metadata.title: Does Inequality Stay in the Shadow? The Cross-national Effects of Educational Equity on Private Tutoring and Student Achievement

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses PISA 2012 student- and school-level microdata (15-year-olds) and supplements it with World Bank nation-level indicators. The authors report using total student weights and 80 replicate weights for the plausible-value-based achievement outcomes (mathematics, science, and reading), following OECD (2013) recommendations. The analytic sample is the full PISA 2012 participating educational-systems sample for which the tutoring and equity indicators are available, with achievement modeled using all five plausible values. The paper does not describe additional ML-specific preprocessing beyond the PV framework; weighting is therefore treated as part of the standard PISA scaling/estimation procedure rather than an ML feature-weighting step.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: The paper states that PISA 2012 achievement uses five plausible values that were multiply-imputed, but it does not explicitly describe the missing-data handling procedure for non-PV variables (e.g., tutoring hours, SES indices, school-quality indices, or World Bank indicators) or whether missing covariates were imputed, excluded, or handled via survey methods. This is a reporting gap because the study relies on multiple questionnaire- and context-derived predictors that can have missingness in PISA microdata. Without the authors’ explicit rule, the robustness of the regression/HLM estimates to missing covariates cannot be fully evaluated.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Used the full available PISA 2012 representative sample of 15-year-old students across the participating educational systems (248,308 students in 16,823 schools across 65 national educational systems, expanding to 83 administrative systems). The study focuses on tutoring participation types (commercial company, personal, family) and models student achievement in mathematics, science, and reading using PISA 2012 plausible values; no additional grade, school-type, or country exclusions are described beyond the World Bank substitution for missing Gini-year values and the exclusion of North America regional grouping to allow variation.

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2012 (15-year-olds) Mathematics achievement (MATH) using 5 plausible values
main_findings.performance_metrics: Weighted linear regression coefficients (all p<.001): COMT b=-2.42 (SE 0.30), PERT b=-5.33 (SE 0.23), FAMT b=-4.59 (SE 0.15); HLM fixed effects (Table 4) show COMT around -0.20 to -0.22 in Models 2/3, PERT around -1.95 to -1.98 (significant), FAMT around -1.55 to -1.59 (significant).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2012 Mathematics achievement the study leveraged commercial, personal, and family tutoring hours together with students’ home possessions and parental education to model mathematics achievement, finding that all three tutoring types are negative predictors in the cross-national weighted regression (e.g., PERT b=-5.33, p<.001). This indicates that, in cross-national PISA 2012 data, private tutoring is more consistent with remediation than enrichment, suggesting that equity-oriented policies should not assume tutoring participation will automatically translate into higher achievement.

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2012 (15-year-olds) Science achievement (SCIE) using 5 plausible values
main_findings.performance_metrics: Weighted linear regression coefficients (all p<.001): COMT b=-2.90 (SE 0.29), PERT b=-5.09 (SE 0.25), FAMT b=-4.19 (SE 0.14); HLM fixed effects (Table 5) show PERT and FAMT negative and significant across models (e.g., PERT about -1.81 to -1.83, FAMT about -1.57 to -1.59), while COMT is largely small/non-significant except in equity-interaction models (e.g., COMT b=-10.21, p<.05).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2012 Science achievement the study leveraged commercial, personal, and family tutoring hours together with students’ home possessions and parental education to model science achievement, finding that all three tutoring types are negative predictors in the cross-national weighted regression (e.g., PERT b=-5.09, p<.001). This indicates that private tutoring participation is not associated with higher science achievement in the pooled cross-national context, implying that policy debates about tutoring as an equity lever should be tempered by evidence of remediation-dominant patterns.

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2012 (15-year-olds) Reading achievement (READ) using 5 plausible values
main_findings.performance_metrics: Weighted linear regression coefficients (all p<.001): COMT b=-2.98 (SE 0.33), PERT b=-4.79 (SE 0.24), FAMT b=-3.92 (SE 0.14); HLM fixed effects (Table 6) show PERT and FAMT negative and significant across models (e.g., PERT about -1.82 to -1.87, FAMT about -1.77 to -1.79), while COMT is negative and significant mainly in equity-interaction models (e.g., COMT b=-13.05, p<.001).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2012 Reading achievement the study leveraged commercial, personal, and family tutoring hours together with students’ home possessions and parental education to model reading achievement, finding that all three tutoring types are negative predictors in the cross-national weighted regression (e.g., COMT b=-2.98, p<.001). This indicates that tutoring participation aligns more with remediation than enrichment across reading outcomes, and that educational equity indicators at school/system levels do not consistently reverse this pattern.

data.outcome_summary: The study analyzes PISA 2012 (15-year-olds) mathematics, science, and reading achievement using five plausible values and applies total student weights with 80 replicate weights, supplemented by World Bank nation-level equity indicators. Across the cross-national weighted regressions, all three private tutoring types (commercial company, personal, family) show negative associations with achievement in every subject (e.g., PERT b=-5.33 in mathematics; COMT b=-2.90 in science; COMT b=-2.98 in reading; all p<.001). Hierarchical linear models further show that tutoring effects often remain negative, while school- and system-level equity indicators have largely non-significant or irregular moderation effects on the tutoring–achievement relationship. The paper does not report any machine-learning model training or predictive metrics; it uses regression/HLM rather than ML algorithms. Because the design is observational and cross-sectional, the negative tutoring coefficients should not be interpreted causally, and missing-data handling for non-PV variables is not fully documented.
